title: Layered Architecture Pattern
oneLiner: Organizes a system into horizontal layers, where each layer depends only on the one directly beneath it.

hero.name: The Foundation
hero.catchphrase: Each layer stands on the one below. Nobody skips a level.
hero.power: Organizes code into strict horizontal layers, each depending only on the layer beneath it, keeping concerns cleanly separated top to bottom.
hero.weakness: Strict layering can force data through layers that don't need to touch it, adding overhead for operations that are really just simple pass-throughs.
hero.origin: The Foundation appeared after a codebase's presentation code was calling raw SQL directly, its business logic was formatting HTML, and every layer touched every other layer, with no order to any of it.

story.problem: Presentation code calls the database directly. Business logic formats HTML. Every part of the system reaches into every other part, with no consistent direction of dependency.
story.solution: The Foundation organizes the system into four strict layers: Presentation → Business Logic → Data Access → Database. Each layer only calls the layer directly below it — never sideways, never skipping levels.
story.result: Dependencies now flow in one predictable direction. The database layer can be swapped without touching presentation code, because nothing above Data Access knows it exists.

before: Any part of the system can call any other part directly
Swapping the database means auditing the entire codebase
after: Each layer only depends on the layer directly beneath it
Dependencies flow in one predictable direction
Swapping the database only touches the Data Access layer

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A dependency graph shows arrows pointing in every direction — presentation calling the database, business logic touching HTML.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I need to swap our database, and I have no idea how many places directly depend on its specific query syntax. Could be anywhere.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Foundation appears, stacking four solid layers, each resting cleanly on the one beneath it.
panels.speaker: The Foundation
panels.dialogue: Stop letting every layer touch every other layer. Stack them — Presentation, Business Logic, Data Access, Database. Each one only knows the layer directly below it.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Presentation calls Business Logic. Business Logic calls Data Access. Data Access talks to the Database. Never the reverse, never sideways.
panels.speaker: The Foundation
panels.dialogue: Dependencies flow in one direction only, top to bottom. Nothing above Data Access even knows which database exists underneath.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The database gets swapped by rewriting exactly one layer. Everything above it is untouched.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We swapped databases by rewriting exactly one layer. Presentation and business logic didn't change at all.

useWhen: You want a clear, predictable direction of dependencies across a moderately complex application.
Different concerns (presentation, business rules, persistence) genuinely need to evolve somewhat independently.
You want the option to swap out infrastructure (database, UI framework) without rewriting the whole system.
avoidWhen: The application is small and simple enough that layering adds ceremony without meaningful benefit.
Strict layer-by-layer calls would force trivial pass-through data through several layers for no real reason.
The team needs the flexibility of a more decoupled style, like hexagonal/ports-and-adapters architecture, that this simpler layering doesn't provide.
commonMistakes: Letting a layer skip past its immediate neighbor to call something two levels down, quietly breaking the strict dependency direction.
Creating circular dependencies between layers, which defeats the whole point of a predictable, one-directional structure.
Over-layering a genuinely simple application, adding indirection with no real payoff.
Confusing Layered Architecture with Facade — layering is a whole-system organizing principle; Facade simplifies access to one specific subsystem.
explanation.realWorldExample: Classic 3-tier (presentation/business/data) enterprise applications, and most 'standard' backend project structures (controllers → services → repositories) are Layered Architecture in practice, whether explicitly named that way or not.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this basically just... good code organization?

conversation.speaker: The Foundation
conversation.message: At its heart, yes — but the discipline matters. The RULE is what makes it powerful: a layer may only depend on the layer directly beneath it. Break that rule even once, and the predictability I offer starts eroding.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When do I add MORE layers than the classic three or four?

conversation.speaker: The Foundation
conversation.message: When a genuinely distinct concern emerges — like a separate integration layer for third-party APIs. But each new layer is a real cost. Don't add one just because it feels tidy.

codeBattle.scenario: Your team's codebase has route handlers directly executing raw SQL queries and formatting HTML in the same function, and a recent database migration required auditing dozens of files scattered across the entire app.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Foundation establishes strict, one-directional layers so a database change is contained entirely within the Data Access layer, instead of rippling through the whole app.

quiz.question: What is the core rule of Layered Architecture?
options: Each layer may only depend on the layer directly beneath it
Every layer can call every other layer freely
There must be exactly three layers, no more, no fewer
Layers communicate only through a message queue
quiz.answer: Each layer may only depend on the layer directly beneath it
quiz.explanation: This strict, one-directional dependency rule is what gives Layered Architecture its predictability.

quiz.question: What benefit does strict layering provide when swapping infrastructure (like a database)?
options: The change is contained to the layer that directly depends on that infrastructure
It automatically migrates all data with zero code changes
It removes the need for any data access layer at all
It makes the swap impossible to ever perform
quiz.answer: The change is contained to the layer that directly depends on that infrastructure
quiz.explanation: Because only the Data Access layer knows about the database, swapping it doesn't ripple upward through the rest of the system.

quiz.question: What's a common violation of Layered Architecture's discipline?
options: A layer skips past its immediate neighbor to call something two levels down
A layer only calls the layer directly beneath it
The presentation layer never touches the database directly
The data access layer doesn't know about the presentation layer
quiz.answer: A layer skips past its immediate neighbor to call something two levels down
quiz.explanation: Layer-skipping breaks the one-directional structure the whole pattern depends on for predictability.

quiz.question: What's a real-world example of Layered Architecture?
options: A classic 3-tier enterprise app with presentation, business logic, and data access layers
A single-file script with no internal structure
quiz.answer: A classic 3-tier enterprise app with presentation, business logic, and data access layers
quiz.explanation: This is the textbook, most widely recognized real-world instance of Layered Architecture.
